clinical_knowledge.topic: Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Refer to multidisciplinary skull base surgical team (neurosurgery and neuro-otology), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive right ear hearing loss, persistent tinnitus, and unsteadiness when walking for 1 year

Key HPI features: 49F presents with 1-year history of slowly worsening right-sided asymmetric hearing loss and high-pitched ringing tinnitus. Over the past 4 months, noticed mild imbalance and veering to the right when walking in the dark, along with occasional right facial numbness and corneal irritation.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 74, BP 120/78. Otoscopic exam reveals clear external canals and normal tympanic membranes. Tuning fork tests show Weber lateralizing to left ear and Rinne positive (AC > BC) bilaterally, confirming right sensorineural hearing loss. Audiogram shows severe right high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with reduced speech discrimination (42%). Decreased right corneal reflex and mild right facial hypesthesia. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrates a 2.2 cm enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle (CPA) with an 'ice cream cone' appearance extending into and widening the internal auditory canal.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cerumen impaction (should be excluded first) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Facial numbness or corneal irritation — signals the tumor is large enough to compress the trigeminal nerve.
management_principles: Refer to multidisciplinary skull base surgical team (neurosurgery and neuro-otology)
2 cm tumor size with brainstem/CN V compression and loss of serviceable hearing, discuss surgical resection via retrosigmoidal or translabyrinthine approach vs Stereotactic Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife)
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 49F presenting with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, ataxia, and early trigeminal sensory involvement suggestive of cerebellopontine angle lesion.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 74, BP 120/78. Otoscopic exam reveals clear external canals and normal tympanic membranes. Tuning fork tests show Weber lateralizing to left ear and Rinne positive (AC > BC) bilaterally, confirming right sensorineural hearing loss. Audiogram shows severe right high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with reduced speech discrimination (42%). Decreased right corneal reflex and mild right facial hypesthesia. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrates a 2.2 cm enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle (CPA) with an 'ice cream cone' appearance extending into and widening the internal auditory canal.
reference_soap.assessment: Right Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma) compressing CN VIII, CN V, and cerebellar peduncle.
reference_soap.plan: Refer to multidisciplinary skull base surgical team (neurosurgery and neuro-otology). Given 2.2 cm tumor size with brainstem/CN V compression and loss of serviceable hearing, discuss surgical resection via retrosigmoidal or translabyrinthine approach vs Stereotactic Radiosurgery (Gamma Knife).

learning_objectives: Identify clinical presentation of cerebellopontine angle tumors (unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, ataxia, CN V/VII deficits)
Interpret audiogram patterns and tuning fork findings (Weber lateralizing to intact ear, Rinne AC > BC) in retrocochlear lesions
Recognize characteristic MRI features of Vestibular Schwannoma (enhancing CPA mass widening internal auditory canal)
Compare management strategies (observation, stereotactic radiosurgery, microsurgical resection) based on tumor size and hearing status

teaching.one_liner: A benign tumor on the hearing/balance nerve causing slowly progressive one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus, and as it grows, imbalance and facial numbness from pressing on neighboring nerves.
red_flags: Facial numbness or corneal irritation — signals the tumor is large enough to compress the trigeminal nerve

history.answer: My right ear has been gradually losing its hearing over the past year, and it feels completely plugged up.
It started about a year ago very gradually, and it has been slowly worsening over time rather than happening suddenly.
It is only affecting my right ear; my left ear still hears normally.
I have significant trouble understanding speech on my right side, especially higher-pitched sounds, and I cannot understand people when holding the phone to that ear.
Yes, my right ear constantly feels plugged and heavy, almost like there is water trapped deep inside.
I have had a constant, high-pitched ringing noise in my right ear for about a year, but it does not pulse with my heartbeat.
I do not experience spinning vertigo, but over the last four months I have felt off-balance and tend to veer to the right, especially in the dark.
No, I have not had any earache, fluid draining, or bleeding from my ears.
No recent cold, sinus congestion, fever, air travel, or scuba diving.
I use cotton swabs gently now and then, but this did not start after swimming or showering.
Over the past four months, the right side of my face feels numb at times, and my right eye gets easily irritated.
No facial drooping, no severe headaches, no limb weakness or numbness, and no difficulty speaking or swallowing.
I teach music at a school, but I have not had any loud industrial noise exposure, gunfire exposure, or loud headphone use.
I have never taken strong IV antibiotics, water pills, chemotherapy medications, or high doses of aspirin.
No, I have never had any head injuries or direct trauma to my ears.
I never had recurrent ear infections as a child, and I have never had ear surgery.
No one in my family had hearing loss at a young age, brain tumors, or genetic nerve conditions.
As a music teacher, it has become difficult to discern tones and teach my classes, and I avoid using my right ear on phone calls.
I was wondering if this might just be chronic earwax impaction deep inside or perhaps fluid buildup in the middle ear.
I am very worried because the ear feels completely plugged and my balance has been deteriorating.
I am hoping to get comprehensive hearing tests and brain imaging to rule out a brain tumor.
I was diagnosed with hypothyroidism about five years ago, but I have no history of high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily every morning, and no over-the-counter drugs or supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine once or twice a month.
I work as a middle school music teacher and live with my husband.
My menstrual cycles are regular, my last menstrual period began two weeks ago, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
The patient appears comfortable, alert, and in no acute distress.
Bilateral external auditory canals are clear without cerumen impaction, and both tympanic membranes are intact and translucent with normal landmarks and no effusion.
Whisper test reveals reduced hearing in the right ear; Weber test lateralizes to the left ear, and Rinne test demonstrates air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally.
Decreased right corneal reflex and mild hypesthesia over the right ophthalmic and maxillary trigeminal distributions are noted, with symmetric facial movements and intact lower cranial nerves.
Tandem walking demonstrates unsteadiness with veering to the right, and Romberg testing shows increased sway with eye closure, while finger-to-nose testing is normal.
No spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus is observed, head impulse testing is normal, and Dix-Hallpike maneuvers do not provoke nystagmus or vertigo.
